ai.definition: Nuclear fusion reactors generate power through the fusion of atomic nuclei under extreme temperatures and pressures, mimicking the processes occurring in stars like the Sun.
ai.howItWorks: Fusion reactions require extremely high temperatures to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between nuclei. This is achieved by heating deuterium and tritium isotopes to millions of degrees Celsius using powerful magnetic fields or lasers. The resulting plasma contains sufficient energy for fusion to occur, releasing helium and a significant amount of energy in the form of heat.
ai.problemSolved: Addressing the global need for sustainable, low-carbon energy sources while reducing dependency on fossil fuels and mitigating climate change impacts.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves complex engineering challenges such as developing materials that can withstand extreme temperatures, creating robust magnetic confinement systems, and ensuring safety protocols are in place to handle radioactive materials and high-energy environments.
ai.buildProcess: Building a fusion reactor requires extensive R&D, material selection, construction of the reactor vessel, installation of magnetic coils, and integration of control systems. Testing phases include plasma generation, heating, and sustained operation at critical conditions.
ai.costDrivers: High initial capital investment, long-term research and development costs, specialized materials, and safety and regulatory compliance expenses drive up overall costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Despite significant advancements, commercial viability remains far off due to technical challenges and lack of operational reactors.
ai.regulation: Stringent safety and environmental regulations are in place, requiring rigorous testing and certification processes before any fusion reactor can be deployed commercially.
ai.risks: Technical risks include achieving sustained plasma conditions, managing high-energy environments, and ensuring the long-term stability of materials under extreme conditions. Financial risks stem from high initial costs and uncertain timelines for commercialization.
ai.profitability: Uncertain due to current lack of operational reactors and ongoing R&D investments. Potential profitability in the future could be significant given the scale of energy production and environmental benefits.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include improvements in plasma confinement techniques, advances in materials science, and breakthroughs in alternative approaches like laser-driven or aneutronic fusion to reduce costs and enhance efficiency.

glossary.def: A stable isotope of hydrogen with one proton and one neutron, used as a fuel in fusion reactors.
A radioactive isotope of hydrogen with one proton and two neutrons, also used as a fuel in fusion reactions.
An ionized gas consisting of free electrons and positive ions, often used to facilitate nuclear fusion processes.
A method for containing plasma using magnetic fields, essential for maintaining the conditions necessary for sustained fusion reactions.

subsystems.name: Confinement system
subsystems.role: holds the fuel together long enough and densely enough to fuse.

subsystems.name: Reaction chamber
subsystems.role: the vacuum vessel or target chamber where fusion happens.

subsystems.name: Fuel system
subsystems.role: supplies deuterium from water and tritium that a plant must breed itself.

subsystems.name: Heating and current drive
subsystems.role: pushes the fuel past the fusion threshold.

subsystems.name: Exhaust and heat removal
subsystems.role: gets the heat out and the helium ash away without melting the walls.

subsystems.name: Control and diagnostics
subsystems.role: keeps an unstable, self-heating plasma stable and detects off-normal events.

buildSteps.title: Choose the confinement route
buildSteps.detail: Magnetic confinement holds a low-density plasma for seconds to minutes; inertial confinement compresses a millimetre fuel pellet for nanoseconds. The engineering that follows is completely different.

buildSteps.title: Design the reaction chamber
buildSteps.detail: The chamber is sized around the plasma or pellet, with ports for heating, fuelling and instruments, and a wall that can survive years of neutron bombardment.

buildSteps.title: Build the magnets or drivers
buildSteps.detail: Superconducting coils are wound from niobium-tin or high-temperature tape and cryogenically cooled; laser or pulsed-power facilities instead need hundreds of precisely aligned beamlines or capacitor banks.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the fuel target or fuelling system
buildSteps.detail: Inertial designs need near-perfect spherical capsules made in their millions; magnetic designs need continuous injection of frozen deuterium-tritium pellets.

buildSteps.title: Install the breeding blanket
buildSteps.detail: Lithium-containing modules surround the plasma to absorb neutrons, make tritium and carry heat to a coolant.

buildSteps.title: Assemble and pump down
buildSteps.detail: Everything is aligned to sub-millimetre tolerance inside a cryostat or target bay, then evacuated to an ultra-high vacuum.

buildSteps.title: Commission with hydrogen
buildSteps.detail: The machine is run first on ordinary hydrogen to prove magnets, alignment and control without producing neutrons.

buildSteps.title: Burn deuterium–tritium
buildSteps.detail: Real fuel is introduced, and the plant must demonstrate that it makes more tritium than it consumes.

buildSteps.title: Generate electricity
buildSteps.detail: Heat is transferred to a steam or helium cycle and a turbine — the step that separates an experiment from a power station.

prerequisites.why: experiments such as JET and the National Ignition Facility proved the physics can work, but not for the long, reliable pulses a plant needs.
high-temperature superconducting tape has been demonstrated at high field; whether full-scale coils survive years of operation is unproven.
fusion neutrons embrittle and activate steel far faster than fission neutrons, and no qualified material exists for a plant lifetime.
a plant must breed, extract and re-inject tritium with very low losses; this has never been demonstrated end to end.
activated components must be replaced by robots, and no plant-scale system has been operated.

pathway.milestone: large public experiments (ITER, NIF, Wendelstein 7-X) and privately funded compact devices are built and run
pathway.unlocks: data on plasma behaviour, materials and tritium handling.

pathway.milestone: machines that reliably produce more fusion power than they consume, in magnetic and inertial designs alike
pathway.unlocks: confidence that a reactor core can be engineered.

pathway.milestone: a demonstration plant with a breeding blanket, remote maintenance and a generator
pathway.unlocks: proof that the whole fuel-and-heat cycle closes.
firm, low-carbon power — conditional on materials and fuel breeding being solved.
